title: Micro electro-mechanical system piezoelectric cantilever array for a broadband vibration energy harvester.

sections.heading: Micro Electro-Mechanical System Piezoelectric Cantilever Array for a Broadband Vibration Energy Harvester
sections.text:
Inwoo Chun1, Hyun-Woo Lee², and Kwang-Ho Kwon1,\*

1Department of Control and Instrumentation Engineering, Korea University, Sejong 339-700, Republic of Korea enivRl

Limited energy sources of ubiquitous sensor networks (USNs) such as fuel cells and batteries have grave drawbacks such as the need for replacements and re-charging owing to their short durability and environmental pollution. Energy harvesting which is converting environmental mechanical vibration into electrical energy has been researched with some piezoelectric materials and various cantilever designs to increase the efficiency of energy-harvesting devices. In this study, we focused on an energy-harvesting cantilever with a broadband vibration frequency. We fabricated a lead zirconate titanate (PZT) cantilever array with various Si proof masses on small beams $5 . 5 \ \mathsf { m m } \times$ $0 . 5 \ \mathsf { m m } \times 0 . 5 \ \mathsf { m m } )$ . We obtained broadband resonant frequencies ranging between $1 2 7 \ H z$ and $1 3 6 ~ \mathsf { H z }$ using a micro electro-mechanical system (MEMS) process. In order to obtain broadband resonant characteristics, the cantilever array was comprised of six cantilevers with different resonant frequencies. We obtained an_output power of about 2.461 $\mu \mathsf { W }$ at an acceleration of $0 . 2 3 ~ \mathfrak { g }$ and a resistance of $4 \ \mathsf { kOmega }$ The measured bandwidth of the resonant frequency was approximately $^ { 9 \ H z }$ (127-136 Hz), which is about six times wider than the bandwidth of a single cantilever.

Keywords: Energy Harvesting, MEMS, Piezoelectric, Broadband Resonance.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Several studies have investigated various energy-harvesting technologies that are used to collect and utilize waste environmental energy, such as solar energy, wind and air power, thermal energy, tidal energy, and mechanical vibration.1-3 These topics have provoked interest because fuel cells and batteries—when used as limitative energy sources for ubiquitous sensor networks (USNs)4, 5_have critical disadvantages, such as their need for replacement and re-charging (due to their short life spans) and their contribution to environmental pollution.69

To increase the efficiency of energy-harvesting devices, energy harvesting—which converts mechanical vibration into electrical energy—has been investigated using piezoelectric materials and various cantilever designs.10 Piezoelectric materials (Perovskite structures) have been used in micro electro-mechanical system (MEMS)- scale cantilevers because these materials can efficiently convert mechanical strain energy into electrical energy without additional power sources. Although many successful demonstrations of large piezoelectric energyharvesting prototypes have been performed, reports on micromachined piezoelectric cantilevers with resonant frequencies in the range of $6 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ are relatively few.116 Generally, environmental vibrations are less than $1 2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ 17

Maximum power can be obtained when the piezoelectric cantilever's resonant frequency matches the frequency of the environmental mechanical vibration. One of the challenges facing piezoelectric cantilevers is the very narrow bandwidth for their resonant frequency (as characterized by their high $Q$ factor). At frequencies further from the resonant frequency, the harvesting power is significantly reduced. Therefore, to ensure that energy can be effectively collected from ambient environments with multiplefrequency spectra, it is crucial to fabricate a harvesting device with a wide operating frequency range.18 To meet this requirement, various methods to tune the resonant frequency have been studied. Most studies seeking to develop a cantilever with broadband frequency resonance have focused on structural design. Kim et al. presented a new design for a compliant, four-bar linkage system that mimics the hair bundle structure inside the inner ear.19 Despite the advantages of this design, a drawback inherent to this type of cantilever is that the proper resonant frequency can be obtained by controlling the frequency, which subsequently requires application of pre-stress to the cantilever.

In the present study, to broaden the bandwidth of the cantilever system, we fabricated a MEMS-scale cantilever array comprised of six cantilevers with different resonant frequencies. The output electrodes were connected in parallel. We tuned the resonant frequency of each individual cantilever by changing the proof-mass length, and we examined the cantilever array's harvested power and resonant frequency behavior using a controlled vibrating system.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.text:
We designed a cantilever array with six cantilevers for a wide resonant frequency range of 125 to $1 3 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ ,which resulted in $9 \mathrm { H z }$ of bandwidth. The resonant frequency was tuned by adjusting the proof-mass lengths.20 In this study, we designed the cantilever using Comsol software (Comsol, Inc., USA), which is a finite-element analysis program for multi-physics processes. This software has a flexible platform that enabled us to model the relevant physical aspects of the cantilever's design.

Figure 1 shows the process flow of the MEMS-scale cantilever, which is a unimorph piezoelectric cantilever array.2,We fabricated thecantlever arryusi MEMS fabrication process similar to a semiconductor process. The cantilever array was fabricated on a silicon-ocinsulator (SOI) wafer with a $1 0 0 \mathrm { - m m }$ diameter. The SOI wafer consisted of three layers: a $1 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick Si (silicon) layer, a $1 - \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer (with silicon dioxide serving as the second etch stop), and a Si substrate layer with a thickness of $5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ About $5 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ in depth, silicon dioxide layers were thermally grown on both sides of the SOI wafer.21 Using magnetron sputtering, a $1 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick Ti (titanium) film and a 100-nm-thick Pt (platinum) film were deposited on the front side of the $5 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer to form the bottom electrode. Because the adhesive force between the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { P t }$ layers is relatively low, a $\mathrm { T i }$ layer was sputtered onto the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ surface. The $1 . 2 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick lead zirconate titanate (PZT) layer was coated using the solgel method. The PZT solution was composed of $\mathrm { P b }$ and $\mathrm { Z r / T i }$ at a formation ratio of $Z \mathrm { r : T i } = 5 2 { : } 4 8$ For the top electrode, a $1 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick Pt layer was deposited by magnetron sputtering. On the SOI wafer, this $\mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { P Z T } / \mathrm { P t } / \mathrm { T i } / \mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ multi-layer was patterned using reactive-ion etching (RIE). The width of the top Pt layer was narrower than the bottom PZT layer's width by almost $0 . 3 \mathrm { \ m m }$ The back-side $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ and Si layerswhich were used as proof masses—were etched down to the SOI wafer's inner $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer using a deep reactive-ion etching (DRIE) system and an inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching (ICP RIE) system.

![](images/f7e97f12b067c76fefaf543f02a3135272d7441e6264554e991e4c2a6634e3e4.jpg)  
Figure 1. Fabrication process of MEMS cantilever device.

![](images/5bd82d11aba70726c99b5e084d12e37269253b67a586bab0b40ea57d17b137e8.jpg)  
Figure 2. Schematic view of the measuring equipment used for the resonant frequency and output voltage measurements of the cantilever array.

ciFigure 2 is a schematic view of the measuring equipment for the resonant frequency and output voltage. The resonant frequency of the fabricated cantilever array was measured using a dynamic signal analyzer (DSA) (35670A, Agilent, USA). The fixed end of the cantilever array was clamped to a shaker, which served as the vibration source. The vibration frequency of the shaker was controlled by the power amplifier, which amplified the signal from the DSA. The output voltage signal was extracted from the voltage generated by vibrational displacement of the cantilever array. Each output voltage from the device was then systematically measured for different vibrational accelerations, vibration frequencies, and resistive loads. Using Ohm's law, the output power was calculated from the voltage across the load resistor connected to the device. The specific load resistance that could extract the maximum output power was called the optimal resistance and was dependent on frequency.23

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Because the proof mass is an important factor for determining a cantilever's resonant frequency, we simulated a cantilever's resonant frequency and mechanical strain using the Comsol simulator. The simulation results were used to determine length of the proof mass and to find the cantilever's resonant frequencies. In our design, the cantilever beams were trapezoidal in shape, which allowed the cantilever to vibrate in the longitudinal direction. The simulation results for the resonant frequencies are shown in Figure 3.

![](images/b214700413d69bc2a5eb3e5630b68699209c7ec2c2d406f372f3d06342e03148.jpg)  
Figure 3. Resonant frequency with mass length of a single cantilever by Comsol simulation.

Figure 3 shows the resonant frequency for the single cantilever with various mass lengths, which were simulated using the Comsol simulator. This figure shows that the resonant frequency decreases from $1 4 8 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 1 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ for a fixed width as the proof-mass length of the cantilever increases from $0 . 7 \mathrm { m m }$ to $1 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m m } .$ An increase in a cantilever's proof-mass length reduces the effective spring constant,23, 24 and this variable directly correlates with the bending modulus per unit width. Consequently, an increase in proof mass leads to a decrease in resonant frequency. This result indicates that mass length is a useful variable for controlling the resonant frequency of a cantilever. Based on these data, we designed a cantilever array. In this work, we fabricated a PZT cantilever array with variable Si proof-mass devices $( \mathrm { l e n g t h } \times \mathrm { w i d t h } \times \mathrm { h e i g h t } = 0 . 9 \ –$ $1 . 1 \ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ with a beam (length $\times$ width $\times$ height $= 5 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 0 1 2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ . In this study, the width was measured at the upper side of the trapezoid. The cantilevers had six different proof masses with resonant frequencies at $1 . 5 { \mathrm { - H } } z$ intervals, which resulted in a broadband resonant frequency span of almost $9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The dimensions of each individual cantilever for the cantilever array were selected to obtain a resonant frequency of about $1 2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ .

Figure 4 shows the fabricated cantilever array with the proof masses. We noted that the cantilever beam could bend due to residual stress. This bending is an important issue for MEMS cantilever systems. The residual stresses in the silicon cantilevers' layers are generated mainly by deposition processes. From this figure, we can see that each cantilever was slightly bent. Despite this bending, the cantilever operated normally under vibration. The cantilevers were parallel-connected, which allowed us to sum the outputs of each individual cantilever.

![](images/652731a9d5c12467d11a3a1c143d5e056ae0f4e5389fb5ee2edf5ea3d7ccd6a6.jpg)  
Figure 4. Photograph of the cantilever energy-harvesting array.

Figure 5 shows the output voltage from the cantilever array measured by the DSA system using an external vibration frequency sweep. This voltage was a root-meansquare (RMS) value measured by the DSA analyzer. The peak voltage values were recalculated by the DSA system. The vibration frequency of the shaker was varied from $1 1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ at an acceleration of $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ (1 g is equivalent to an acceleration of $9 . 8 \mathrm { \ m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ ). The measured bandwidth of the resonant frequency was approximately $9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ $1 2 7 { - } 1 3 6 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . This bandwidth was in close agreement with the Comsol simulated value and resulted in an error of less than $10 \%$ The output characteristics showed broadened_resonant behavior with a small intra-peak2 structure located at the corresponding resonant frequency of each single cantilever. As designed, the bandwidth of the array was about six times wider than the bandwidth of a single cantilever. We could also see that the voltage output on the high side of the resonant frequency rapidly decreased with increasing frequency. Simultaneously, the highest intra-peak value of the output voltage was observed on the low side of the resonant frequency, and the output was higher at these frequencies than the output on the high side of the resonant frequency.

![](images/fa63a11ed1257e9cf8e5faadcd4623c5e3038d60c2294b80561aae8e83db7ee9.jpg)  
Figure 5. Output voltage of cantilever array with a vibration frequency sweep at $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ $\mathrm { \mathit { g } = 9 . 8 \ m / s ^ { 2 } }$

![](images/b7e3a63588ba29ca034ca4b03c99a893d86be5052575e3ce0b282d65a3428401.jpg)  
Figure 6. Output power of the cantilever array as a function of load resistance at $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ .

These asymmetric behaviors occurred because—compared with higher frequencies—more waveforms overlapped at lower frequencies due to the asymmetric characteristics of each individual cantilever's waveforms.

Figure 6 shows both the voltage and the power output of the cantilever array as a function of load resistance. This measurement was conducted at a vibrating acceleration of $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ with a fixed resonant frequency of $1 3 1 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . This frequency was selected to correspond to the mean of the maximum and minimum voltages. The output voltage with various resistive loads was measured, and the output power was calculated using Ohm's law. The output voltage increased sharply until the load resistance reached approximately $4 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .Above this value, the output voltage was nearly saturated, although the resistance increased. Furthermore, the maximum output power was obtained at a resistance of $4 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , and this finding indicates that the internal impedance of the cantilever array was approximately $4 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

In our previous research, we fabricated a single cantilever with Si proof-mass devices $\mathrm { ( l e n g t h \times w i d t h \times }$ height $= 1 . 5 ~ \mathrm { { \ m m } \times 0 . 4 8 ~ \mathrm { { \ m m } \times 0 . 4 5 ~ \mathrm { { \ m m } ) } } }$ with a beam $( \mathrm { l e n g t h } \times \mathrm { w i d t h } \times \mathrm { h e i g h t } = 2 . 4 5 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 4 8 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times$ $0 . 0 1 2 \ \mathrm { m m }$ . The bandwidth of the single cantilever was measured to be approximately $1 { - } 2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ Compared with a single cantilever in our previous study (for which the output power was approximately $0 . 1 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at the optimal resistance of $4 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , while the acceleration was $0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { g }$ , the output power and bandwidth increased dramatically in the present study.21

Figure 7 shows the output power of the cantilever array as a function of the vibration frequency with various gravitational accelerations ranging from $0 . 2 3 \textrm { g }$ to $0 . 7 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ at a resistance of $4 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .The output power increased with an increase in acceleration. This result was unsurprising because higher accelerations can induce a larger deformation in the cantilever. We obtained a maximum output power of about $1 6 . 6 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and a minimum output power of about $5 . 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $0 . 7 ~ g$ , and the optimal resistance was $4 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . We realized a broadband energy-harvesting system with a bandwidth of $9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ The output power at $0 . 2 3 \mathrm { ~ g ~ }$ had almost same shape as the output voltage at $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ ,as shown in Figure 5. At a resistance of $4 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , the output power attained a maximum power of about $3 . 8 6 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at an acceleration of $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ , and this power corresponds to a peak voltage of $3 . 9 3 2 ~ \mathrm { m V } .$ Our MEMS-scale cantilever array could respond to a small vibration of $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ .

![](images/bb4e470cc32cc8fde2a88d9fc236a437292e5152e6523bde941dbdee9aed43e4.jpg)  
Figure 7. Output power of the cantilever array as a function of vibration frequency at various gravitational accelerations.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
This study investigated the design and characteristics of a vibration energy harvester based on a MEMSscale piezoelectric cantilever array comprised of six cantilevers with different resonant frequencies. We fabricated a PZT cantilever array with variable-area Si proofmass devices $( \mathrm { l e n g t h } \times \mathrm { w i d t h } \times \mathrm { h e i g h t } = 0 . 9 \mathrm { - } 1 . 1 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times$ $0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ using a MEMS process with a small fixed beam size $\mathrm { l e n g t h \times w i d t h \times h e i g h t = 5 . 5 ~ m m \times }$ $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 0 1 2 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ ). We successfully fabricated MEMSscale cantilevers with integrated variable proof masses for a broadband resonant frequency. We compared experimental results with resonant frequency simulations obtained using Comsol software. In Comsol simulations, the resonant frequency was simulated in accordance with the proof-mass length increasing from $0 . 9 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $0 . 1 1 \mathrm { ~ m m }$ with a fixed beam length. The bandwidth was found to be between $1 2 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ and $1 3 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ ,In measuring the internal resistance, it was confirmed that the internal impedance of the cantilever array was $4 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .At this resistance, the output power was about $3 . 8 6 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at an acceleration of $0 . 2 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ , which corresponded to a peak voltage of $3 . 9 3 2 \mathrm { m V } .$ Furthermore, the measured bandwidth at the resonant frequency was approximately $9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ $1 2 7 \mathrm { - } 1 3 6 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ , which is about six times wider than the bandwidth of the single cantilever.
